articles.title: Advances in click-enabled dendrimers: bridging molecular engineering, biomedical applications, and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Dendrimers are highly branched, multivalent macromolecules with generation-dependent architectures that can be prepared with comparatively well-defined molecular compositions. Their architecture and synthetic tunability enable controlled incorporation of targeting ligands, therapeutic agents, imaging probes, and stimuli-responsive functionalities within a single nanoscale construct. These attributes distinguish dendrimers from many conventional nanocarriers and support their investigation as multifunctional platforms for advanced therapeutic applications. However, broader translation of dendrimer technologies has been hindered by challenges associated with synthetic complexity, manufacturing costs, purification and characterization requirements, large-scale reproducibility, predictable biological performance, and increasingly stringent regulatory expectations for advanced nanomedicines. Click chemistry provides one strategy for addressing some of these synthetic and functionalization limitations by enabling expedited and orthogonal dendrimer construction and further modification. Copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC), strain-promoted azide-alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC), inverse electron-demand Diels-Alder (IEDDA), thiol-ene, thiol-yne, and related bioorthogonal reactions have expanded the ways in which dendrimers can be synthesized and drugs, targeting ligands, imaging agents, nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and stimuli-responsive linkers can be incorporated into these scaffolds with greater structural control. This review examines click-enabled dendrimers for various biomedical applications. Emphasis is placed on how dendrimer generation, surface charge, ligand density, linker chemistry, degradability, and click reaction choice influence biological performance and translational potential. Marketed and clinically evaluated dendrimer technologies are also discussed to highlight the design, manufacturing, and characterization requirements needed for broader clinical adoption.

articles.title: Mitochondrial Fatty Acid Oxidation Dysregulation in Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease: Mechanistic Roles and Emerging Diagnostic and Therapeutic Advances.
articles.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease is a chronic metabolic liver disorder driven by the convergent effects of obesity, insulin resistance, lipid overload, gut-liver axis disruption, and immune inflammation. Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation is central to the disposal of excess fatty acids and the maintenance of hepatocellular energy homeostasis; under sustained metabolic stress, however, this process can shift from an adaptive response to a molecular hub for incomplete oxidation, oxidative injury, inflammatory amplification, and fibrotic progression. This review examines fatty acid uptake and activation, carnitine-dependent transport, sequential β-oxidation, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, electron transfer, mitochondrial quality control, and immunometabolic crosstalk, and explains how diet, circadian disruption, aging, gut dysbiosis, drug exposure, and genetic susceptibility destabilize oxidative homeostasis through defined molecular pathways. From a translational perspective, we propose a functional-endotype framework that integrates imaging, acylcarnitine profiling, lipidomics, oxidative-damage markers, inflammatory and fibrotic indices, and genetic risk to guide stratified interventions targeting thyroid hormone signaling, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors, incretin pathways, bile-acid signaling, fibroblast growth factors, energy-sensing networks, and precision nanomedicine.

articles.title: Immunogenicity risk assessment of novel modalities using new approach methodologies.
articles.abstract: A new generation of medicines that includes gene therapies, cell-based treatments and gene editors have the potential to treat a vast range of diseases. However, the clinical success of these novel modalities is limited by unwanted immune responses, which can compromise both safety and efficacy. Regulatory agencies have recently emphasized reducing animal testing in preclinical safety studies and envisioned a strategic approach for basing regulatory decisions on scientifically validated new approach methodologies (NAMs). These methods encompass mathematical models, artificial intelligence tools, organ-on-a-chip systems, and advanced in vitro and ex vivo assays. In combination, these approaches seem potentially well suited for assessing unwanted immune responses of the novel modalities. Key challenges to be addressed include predicting the immunogenicity risks from transgene products, delivery vehicles and gene-editing machinery; managing pre-existing immunity; overcoming barriers to repeat dosing; and establishing robust long-term monitoring strategies. In this Perspective, we critically evaluate how the current NAMs toolkit, originally developed for protein therapeutics, can be adapted to assess the unwanted immune responses of novel modalities. We provide a forward-looking framework for developing and validating the next generation of predictive immunogenicity tools required to safely unlock the full therapeutic potential of these revolutionary medicines.

articles.title: Emerging HER2-targeted treatment approaches for gastroesophageal cancer in the era of chemo-immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a key therapeutic target in gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA) and its targeting agents form the backbone of treatment for HER2-positive disease. Therapeutic options have expanded from the HER2-targeting antibody trastuzumab to antibody-drug conjugates (ADC). HER2-directed small-molecule inhibitors and bispecific HER2-directed compounds are under evaluation in treatment-naive and previously treated patients across different stages of disease. Beyond combinations with chemotherapy, combinations with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) are of particular interest due to potential synergistic mechanisms, including antigen release, immune-cell recruitment, and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity resulting in enhanced antitumor immunity. The current standard of care for HER2- and PD-L1-positive metastatic GEA (mGEA) combines chemotherapy with the HER2-targeting antibody trastuzumab and the PD-1-targeting ICI pembrolizumab. In the second-line setting, the ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan has further improved outcomes for these patients. Despite these advances and the emergence of new therapeutic options, several challenges remain, including optimal patient and drug selection, treatment sequencing, and the management of acquired resistance. Advances in liquid biopsy approaches, including the analysis of circulating tumor DNA, may facilitate longitudinal disease monitoring and guide personalized treatment strategies. This review summarizes the current and evolving role of HER2-targeted therapies in GEA, examines the growing integration of immunotherapy, and discusses future directions.

articles.title: Toward precision nanomedicine via artificial intelligence guided design and prediction.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is advancing nanomedicine development by linking formulation variables and biological context with delivery, therapeutic efficacy, and safety. This review examines AI assisted formulation design, centralized formulation databases, prediction of nanoparticle self assembly, and models of cell and tissue selective delivery, biodistribution, and therapeutic outcomes. Recent advances in predicting nanotoxicity and nanoparticle induced immune responses further emphasize the importance of incorporating safety endpoints into nanomedicine optimization. Beyond nanocarrier engineering, foundation models and multimodal analyses of single-cell and spatial data are expanding biological discovery by characterizing disease associated cellular states, prioritizing therapeutic targets, and predicting treatment responses. Computational approaches also support the design of therapeutic RNA, peptides, proteins, and programmable protein nanomaterials. For example, mRNA sequences generated by GEMORNA and delivered via lipid nanoparticles increased erythropoietin expression in mice by up to 15-fold compared with a benchmark sequence. Integration of biological discovery with biomolecular and nanocarrier design may inform therapeutic cargo selection, targeting strategies, and functional nanomaterial development. AI may connect patient specific biological characteristics with predictions of nanomedicine delivery and therapeutic response to support patient stratification and individualized treatment selection. Integration of histological, imaging, molecular, and longitudinal data may enable treatment strategies to be adapted to differences in tissue characteristics, disease state, and therapeutic response. Emerging approaches based on digital twins and adaptive treatment control may extend the framework toward individualized dosing and dynamic treatment optimization. Major challenges include data heterogeneity, limited model generalizability, and the need for experimental and prospective validation. Progress toward precision therapy will require integrated frameworks that jointly consider delivery, efficacy, selectivity, and safety while clearly distinguishing demonstrated applications from future opportunities.

articles.title: Stromal Immune Niches in Transplantation: Signaling Circuits and Therapeutic Targets beyond Lymphoid Organs.
articles.abstract: Stromal cells, the extracellular matrix (ECM), and vascular and lymphatic networks are increasingly recognized as organizers of local immune responses in solid organ grafts. However, transplant immunology remains centered largely on immune cells and lymphoid tissues. Here we propose the graft stromal immune niche as an operational concept: a spatially restricted microenvironment in which local stromal, vascular, lymphatic, or matrix-derived cues are associated with measurable changes in immune-cell localization, persistence, differentiation, or function. Synthesizing evidence from kidney, heart, lung, and liver grafts, we describe three recurring spatial contexts-perivascular, interface-associated, and perilymphatic/egress-associated-and discuss how early injury, ECM mechanics, and stromal programming may shape niche behavior over time. Building on current evidence, we propose a three-state model encompassing rejection-prone, tolerance-permissive, and fibrotic niches; delineate established knowledge and remaining evidence gaps; and critically evaluate pharmacological interventions at different stages of clinical development. This framework is intended to guide the interpretation of spatial datasets and the design of niche-directed strategies.

articles.title: Bacteria-inspired drug delivery systems for cancer immunotherapy: from exploiting to mimicking.
articles.abstract: Bacteria possess distinctive properties, including preferential tumor colonization, motility, immune stimulation, and genetic tractability, which provide opportunities for drug delivery and cancer immunotherapy. These properties have supported the development of living bacteria-based delivery systems that transport therapeutic cargo, produce therapeutic agents locally, and regulate antitumor immune responses. Herein, we review the therapeutic mechanisms and design strategies of these systems, focusing on how bacterial natural characteristics enhance delivery efficiency, enable cargo loading, and control in situ therapeutic production and release. We also discuss how administration routes influence their delivery performance and therapeutic outcomes. Building on these advances, we examine bacteria-inspired biomimetic delivery systems that reproduce selected bacterial structures and functions, including morphology, surface recognition and adhesion, and navigation mechanisms. By combining these features with defined materials, biomimetic systems may improve targeting and tissue penetration while reducing replication-associated infection risks and improving control over composition and immune stimulation. Finally, we compare the capabilities and limitations of living bacterial platforms and biomimetic systems and discuss their distinct safety concerns and translational requirements. This review connects the exploitation of living bacterial characteristics with biomimetic design and identifies priorities for developing bacteria-inspired cancer immunotherapies.

articles.title: Natural products as modulators of the NLRP3 inflammasome: mechanisms of action, chemical diversity, and therapeutic potential.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: The NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome is a cytosolic multiprotein signaling platform that coordinates caspase-1 activation, interleukin-1β (IL-1β) and IL-18 maturation, and pyroptosis following infection or tissue injury. Its dysregulation contributes to diverse inflammatory diseases. Natural products offer structurally diverse scaffolds for NLRP3 modulator discovery. PURPOSE: This review evaluates natural products that inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome activation, with emphasis on their chemical diversity, direct and indirect mechanisms, structure-activity relationships, and translational limitations. METHODS: PubMed and Web of Science were searched from database inception through July, 2026 using combinations of "NLRP3" with "natural compounds", "traditional Chinese medicine", or "Chinese herbal medicine". Manual screening identified 46 structurally defined compounds with experimental evidence of NLRP3 regulation. Clinical trial registries were searched through July 2026 for NLRP3-targeting agents in clinical development. RESULTS: The 46 natural compounds comprised alkaloids, terpenoids, flavonoids, and phenolic compounds. Their reported mechanisms included direct engagement of NLRP3, interference with NLRP3-NEK7-dependent inflammasome assembly, and indirect modulation of NF-κB-dependent priming, oxidative and mitochondrial stress, ion fluxes, autophagy, and mitophagy. Direct target engagement was supported for only a limited subset, whereas most compounds acted through upstream pathways. Clinical development was dominated by synthetic inhibitors, while clinical validation of natural-product-derived NLRP3 modulators remained limited. CONCLUSION: Natural products represent a promising source of NLRP3 inflammasome modulators and lead scaffolds for anti-inflammatory drug discovery. Further studies should establish target engagement and selectivity, characterize pharmacokinetic and safety profiles, and validate efficacy in clinically relevant models to support clinical translation.

articles.title: Lesion-targeting and vascular matrix-penetrating siRNA nanotherapeutics for the treatment of abdominal aortic aneurysm.
articles.abstract: Inefficient aneurysmal aorta enrichment and vascular matrix penetration represent major challenges against siRNA delivery for the management of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). Herein, platelet membrane (PM)-reversibly camouflaged nanocomplexes (NCs) are developed to deliver Poldip2 siRNA (siPoldip2) into vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs), which then restore vascular homeostasis by promoting phenotypic switching and mitigating oxidative stress. The NCs comprise a cationic nanocore assembled from siPoldip2 and a guanidinated and fluorinated bifunctional helical polypeptide (8FP), a charge-reversal intermediate layer of poly(l-lysine)-cis-aconitic acid (PC), and an outer shell of PM. After systemic administration in CaCl2-induced AAA rats, the NCs could preferentially accumulate at the aneurysmal site due to PM-mediated recognition of RGD-containing extracellular matrix proteins. The slightly acidic aneurysmal microenvironment subsequently triggers charge reversal of PC from negative to positive, which promotes the detachment of both PM and PC layers. The exposed 8FP/siPoldip2 nanocore penetrates the vascular matrix due to fluorocarbon-assisted repulsion of collagen mesh adsorption, followed by effective internalization by VSMCs. Consequently, Poldip2 expression in VSMCs is downregulated, which restores the contractile phenotype, and improves the aortic elasticity as well as structural integrity. This study provides a promising strategy for overcoming vascular delivery barriers and highlights the therapeutic promise of siRNA-based medical intervention for AAA.

articles.title: A model-informed strategy for long-acting PLGA microspheres: Dog-to-human translation and model-to-model correlation using brexpiprazole as a model drug.
articles.abstract: Despite the clinical success of long-acting injectable (LAI) formulations, their development still relies heavily on empirical optimization, which provides limited mechanistic understanding or predictive translation between in vitro and in vivo performance. This study aimed to develop a model-informed strategy for long-acting PLGA microspheres that integrates PopPK modeling and model-to-model correlation to support dog-to-human translation and quantitatively link in vitro release with model-predicted human absorption, using brexpiprazole (BPZ) as a model drug. Monodisperse BPZ-loaded microspheres were prepared via cross-flow membrane emulsification and exhibited a narrow size distribution (span value ≤0.57). In vitro release studies revealed viscosity-dependent biphasic profiles, and pharmacokinetic (PK) studies in Beagle dogs demonstrated consistent rank-order release kinetics and prolonged systemic exposure with increasing polymer viscosity. Because of pronounced interspecies differences in BPZ pharmacokinetics between dogs and humans, PopPK modeling and simulation were used to characterize and compare the PK profiles of BPZ after administration of the oral reference tablet and BPZ-loaded microspheres. The dog PK model was extrapolated to humans using clinically reported and appropriately scaled PK parameters of BPZ. The resulting model-predicted human PK profiles were subsequently employed to establish a model-to-model correlation between in vitro release and model-predicted human absorption. The correlation showed good internal consistency, with prediction errors (%PE) below 10%, indicating a close quantitative relationship between the two model-derived profiles. Overall, this study provides proof of concept for a quantitative, model-informed framework that integrates in vitro release, animal pharmacokinetics, interspecies extrapolation and model-to-model correlation between in vitro release and model-predicted human absorption. This approach highlights the potential of model-informed drug development (MIDD) to improve translational predictability and guide the rational design of LAI antipsychotics.

articles.title: Computer vision-aided locomotor behavioral analysis identifies therapeutic motor signatures in a mouse model of Huntington's disease.
articles.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor dysfunction. Traditional open-field tests quantify spontaneous locomotor parameters but provide limited information on the duration and sequencing of individual movements across HD stages. Here, we applied a computer vision-aided behavioral flow analysis to quantify fine, HD-relevant motor dysfunction in the zQ175DN HD mouse model, from early to developed HD motor deficits. With DeepLabCut-tracked body movements, Keypoint-MoSeq identified recurrent behavioral syllables through unsupervised segmentation of standard top-view open-field recordings. These syllables were then grouped into behavioral clusters and analyzed for transitions between movements. Disease stage-dependent syllable occurrence and transition structure changes were identified. Genotype classification using syllable mean duration showed insufficient discrimination at 6 months and modest discrimination at 9 months, and combined behavioral features yielded higher discrimination at 12 months. HD was also associated with changes in which behavioral clusters served as hubs in the transition networks and the probabilities of switching between behaviors. We integrated these features into an HD motor dysfunction (HDMD) score based on deviations from age-matched wild-type (WT) reference values. The HDMD score distinguished zQ175DN mice from WT at multiple HD stages and aligned with HD pathology and disease severity. This HDMD scoring system may support retrospective analysis and more efficient preclinical drug-study design, as suggested by preliminary effect-size and power estimates assuming partial normalization of the HD phenotype. Overall, the HDMD score summarizes subtle motor abnormalities in HD mice and indicates further validation for preclinical drug efficacy assessment.

articles.title: PIAS1 mitigates vascular calcification through regulating mitochondrial DNA leakage mediated by VDAC1-NLRX1 axis in diabetic models.
articles.abstract: Vascular calcification, an important pathological process of cardiovascular remodeling, is primarily driven by the transition of vascular smooth muscle cells from contractile to osteogenic phenotype. Protein inhibitor of activated STAT1 (PIAS1) is closely associated with diabetes and vascular diseases, but its role and underlying mechanisms in the progression of diabetic vascular calcification (DVC) remain unclear. Herein, we investigated the role of PIAS1 in DVC by genetic modulation and explored its molecular mechanisms by transcriptomics and co-immunoprecipitation with mass spectrometry (Co-IP-MS). We demonstrate that PIAS1 expression is downregulated in both in vitro and in vivo DVC models; furthermore, PIAS1 overexpression alleviates DVC, whereas PIAS1 knockout exacerbates it. Mechanistically, Co-IP-MS analysis reveals an interaction between PIAS1 and voltage-dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1), which enhances the SUMOylation of VDAC1 while inhibiting its oligomerization. PIAS1 also reduces the binding between NLR family member X1 (NLRX1) and VDAC1, ultimately attenuating mitochondrial DNA leakage into the cytoplasm. More importantly, we find that Ginsenoside Ro is a PIAS1-targeting natural product which alleviates DVC. These findings identify PIAS1 as a novel therapeutic target for DVC and provide a new candidate for DVC prevention and treatment.

articles.title: Targeting ELF3 with Biomimetic Nanotherapy Sensitizes PDAC to Gemcitabine via GSDME-mediated Pyroptosis.
articles.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) continues to be a lethal malignancy with limited effective treatment strategies due to modest intrinsic response to systemic chemotherapy. Moreover, the dense, fibrotic stroma and poor vasculature of pancreatic tumors severely restrict drug penetration and therapeutic efficacy. The transcription factor ELF3 acts as a key oncogenic driver that promotes tumor growth, metastasis, and chemoresistance. To address these delivery barriers and enhance therapeutic response, we developed a biomimetic nanoplatform using cancer cell membrane-coated ZIF-8 nanoparticles (CNPs) to co-deliver gemcitabine (GEM) and an ELF3-targeting shRNA (shELF3), aiming to improve tumor-targeting specificity and elucidate the underlying cell death mechanism. Efficient encapsulation of GEM and shRNA ELF3 within a biomimetic nanocarrier was successfully confirmed. In vitro evaluation demonstrated that GEM/shELF3-CNPs activated canonical caspase-3/gasdermin E (GSDME)-dependent pyroptosis, resulting in markedly enhanced cytotoxicity in 6606 PDA cells. Furthermore, in vivo administration yielded superior tumor accumulation, potent tumor growth suppression, and significantly prolonged survival in the murine PDAC model, alongside favorable biosafety profiles. Our findings demonstrate that combining ELF3 silencing with gemcitabine delivery via biomimetic nanocarriers presents a promising synergistic strategy to sensitize pancreatic tumors and enhance PDAC therapeutic outcomes. The graphical representation of the study is shown in Fig. 1.

articles.title: Atractylenolide I promotes white matter repair and neurological recovery after ischemic stroke via ER-dependent microglial activation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: White matter injury following ischemic stroke contributes substantially to persistent neurological disability, yet effective pharmacological strategies that promote post-stroke repair remain limited. Atractylenolide I (ATR-I), a bioactive sesquiterpene lactone from Atractylodes macrocephala Koidz, is anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective, but its role in white matter repair and its direct target are unknown. PURPOSE: To determine whether ATR-I promotes post-stroke white matter repair and neurological recovery and to elucidate its underlying mechanism. METHODS: ATR-I was evaluated in transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) mice and BV-2 microglia/OLN93 oligodendrocyte precursor cell (OPC) conditioned-medium experiments. Neurological function, white matter integrity, microglial polarization, and OPC differentiation were assessed by immunostaining, electron microscopy, and BrdU tracing; molecular docking, surface plasmon resonance (SPR), and fulvestrant blockade tested direct ERα/ERβ binding. RESULTS: ATR-I improved long-term motor and cognitive function and preserved white matter integrity after MCAO. It shifted microglia marker from pro-inflammatory (CD16/32⁺, iNOS⁺) toward reparative (CD206⁺) phenotypes and selectively promoted OPC differentiation over proliferation, an effect exerted indirectly through microglial paracrine signaling. Mechanistically, ATR-I directly bound ERα and ERβ (docking- and SPR-confirmed), upregulated both receptors in microglia, increased the expression of the co-repressor CtBP, and suppressed NF-κΒ signaling. ER blockade with fulvestrant abolished these cellular and functional benefits, confirming that these effects are ER-dependent. CONCLUSIONS: ATR-I promotes post-stroke white matter repair and neurological recovery by targeting ER signaling to regulate microglial activation and facilitate OPC differentiation. These findings support ATR-I as a promising therapeutic candidate for ischemic stroke.

articles.title: CARM1 orchestrates hypoxia-mediated chemoresistance through the H3R17me2a/FUS upregulation in colorectal cancer.
articles.abstract: Hypoxia drives chemoresistance in colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the underlying epigenetic mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we identify CARM1 as a key mediator of this response. Single-cell sequencing and patient cohort analysis show that CARM1 is overexpressed in malignant epithelial cells and correlates with poor prognosis. Mechanistically, hypoxia transcriptionally upregulates CARM1 via activation of the ERK-EGR1 signaling pathway, while concomitantly suppressing dual-specificity phosphatase 2 (DUSP2) to sustain the activation of this axis. Forced expression of wild-type but not phosphatase-dead (C257S) DUSP2 abrogated ERK-EGR1-mediated CARM1 induction. Functionally, elevated levels of CARM1 contribute to drug resistance, while knockout of CARM1 sensitized both p53 wild-type (HCT116) and p53 mutant (HT-29) cells to chemotherapy. Chromatin immunoprecipitation PCR demonstrated that CARM1-mediated asymmetric dimethylation of histone 3 arginine 17 at the FUS promoter upregulates FUS expression, thereby promoting drug resistance by reducing genotoxic stress-induced DNA damage. Notably, oxaliplatin-resistant cells, which also exhibit cross-resistance to 5-fluorouracil, maintain high CARM1/FUS levels via sustained DUSP2 suppression even in normoxia, indicating that drug-resistant cancer cells phenotypically share signaling features with hypoxia-adapted cells to maintain chemoresistance. Pharmacological inhibition of CARM1 with EZM2302 disrupted this axis and enhanced the chemotherapeutic efficacy in refractory orthotopic mouse models. Our findings demonstrate that the EGR1-CARM1-FUS axis is a critical driver of CRC chemoresistance and a potential therapeutic target.

articles.title: ER stress-induced chaperone-assisted selective autophagy confers resistance to mitotic catastrophe-driven anticancer effects by degrading toxic protein aggregates to inhibit caspase-2 activation.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Polyploidization frequently occurs following cell cycle arrest induced by microtubule-targeting agents (MTAs); however, it remains unclear whether this process is beneficial or detrimental to cancer treatment. METHODS: The fate of MTAs-induced polyploid cells was determined using inhibitors of different cell death modalities and live-cell imaging. Western blotting, immunofluorescence, puromycin incorporation assay, flow cytometry, and co-immunoprecipitation were employed to elucidate the mechanisms of cell death pathways regulated upon mitotic catastrophe. Tumor tissues of patients and mice were analyzed to verify the anticancer mechanisms of mitotic catastrophe. RESULTS: Cell polyploidization induced by MTAs is a hallmark of mitotic catastrophe, which is a special mechanism of cell death. Cell death upon mitotic catastrophe is regulated by caspase-2 activation triggered by proteotoxic stress. However, the prolonged duration of this cell death process, relative to other cell death modalities, impedes the exploitation of mitotic catastrophe in cancer treatment. Proteotoxic stress is caused by endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress activation via the accumulation of polyubiquitinated proteins that arising from both increased production and insufficient UPS-mediated degradation. The activation of caspase-2 depends on RAIDD rather than the PIDDosome. Surprisingly, ER stress plays paradoxically dual roles, as it both promotes and delays cell death during mitotic catastrophe. ER stress activates chaperone-assisted selective autophagy (CASA) via the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4 pathway, thereby driving aggresomes formation, upregulating HSP70 and HSPB8 to recruit BAG3, and assembling the CASA complex. The toxic protein aggregates are sequestered into aggresomes, transported via autophagosomes, fused with lysosomes and finally degraded by CASA. Targeted inhibition of CASA could be an effective strategy for enhancing mitotic catastrophe-driven anticancer effects. CONCLUSION: This study elucidates the regulatory mechanisms of mitotic catastrophe-driven cell death following MTAs treatment, identifies potential therapeutic targets to overcome the resistance to mitotic catastrophe, and provides a theoretical basis for optimizing therapeutic strategies that exploit mitotic catastrophe as an anticancer modality.

articles.title: Model-Informed Evaluation of Drug-Drug Interaction Recommendations for Amlodipine and Nirmatrelvir-Ritonavir: A Hypothesis-Generating Analysis.
articles.abstract: While nirmatrelvir-ritonavir effectively prevents severe COVID-19, its ritonavir component causes significant drug-drug interactions (DDIs). Current guidelines suggest mitigating this interaction by halving the amlodipine dose or moving to every-other-day (EOD) dosing, then resuming the standard regimen 3-5 days post-antiviral treatment. We applied physiologically based pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PBPK-PD) modeling to evaluate the effects of these recommendations on systolic blood pressure (SBP) control. SARS-CoV-2 inpatients who received nirmatrelvir-ritonavir (October-December 2022) and were exposed to potential DDIs were identified. An amlodipine PBPK-PD model incorporating the diurnal variation of SBP was developed. The model was validated using amlodipine PK studies, including in DDI scenarios, while the PD model was validated against SBP data collected during amlodipine treatment. Simulations were performed in representative virtual populations, comprising various amlodipine doses and regimens, during and after nirmatrelvir-ritonavir therapy. 362/1729 (20.9%) drugs from 166/217 (76.5%) patients were identified to have potential DDIs implicating nirmatrelvir-ritonavir. Amlodipine was a common interacting drug (64/362, 17.7%) and often prescribed without dose adjustment (63%). Our simulations supported that continuing amlodipine during therapy may lead to SBP ≤100 mmHg at daily doses of ≥5 mg, while discontinuation may lead to SBP >130-150 mmHg. Halving the amlodipine dose during nirmatrelvir-ritonavir treatment could provide more stable SBP control than EOD dosing. Resuming usual doses 3 days after nirmatrelvir-ritonavir could be more important in those receiving 7.5 and 10 mg of amlodipine. DDIs between nirmatrelvir-ritonavir and amlodipine were common. Our simulations evaluated current dose adjustment recommendations for amlodipine with mechanistic quantitative reasoning.

articles.title: Therapeutic potential of escin and its nanoparticle formulations in cancer -a systematic review and meta-analysis of preclinical study.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The present study aimed to perform a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the potential therapeutic effects and underlying mechanisms of Escin and its nanoparticle formulations in cancer based on preclinical studies. METHODS: English databases including PubMed, Web of Science and Embase were used to search all relevant articles from their inception to July 13, 2026. The risk of bias of the included studies was assessed using the SYRCLE animal experiment risk assessment tool, while Review Manager (RevMan) software (Version 5.4) and Stata SE 12 software were employed for all statistical computations. Egger's test was used to assess potential publication bias. RESULTS: The initial search produced a total of 279 potentially pertinent studies, and 34 studies met the inclusion criteria. The meta-analysis findings demonstrated Escin significantly inhibited cancer cell growth in vitro. Compared with the control group, Escin substantively reduced cell viability (SMD = -4.73, 95% CI = [-5.81, -3.65]), induced cell cycle arrest (SMD = -7.29, 95% CI = [-10.45, -4.14]), increased cell apoptosis (SMD =4.88, 95% CI = [3.41, 6.36]), and inhibited cell colony formation (SMD = -8.15, 95% CI = [-14.04, -2.26]), cell adhesion (SMD = -11.17, 95% CI = [-17.80, -4.55]), and migration (SMD = -3.19, 95% CI = [-4.80, -1.57]). In tumor-bearing animals, Escin treatment reduced tumor weight (SMD =-2.49, 95% CI = [-3.27, -1.70]), tumor volume (SMD = -2.05, 95% CI = [-2.87, -1.23]), and tumor number (SMD = -1.83, 95% CI = [-2.84, -0.82]). Besides, Escin nanoformulations also significantly reduced cell viability (SMD = -3.12, 95% CI = [-5.15, -1.09]). DISCUSSION: Overall, this meta-analysis provided quantitative preclinical evidence supporting the potential anti-tumor effects of Escin and its nanoformulations. However, given the heterogeneity and limited number of included studies, especially for nanoformulations, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Further well-designed preclinical studies are warranted to facilitate clinical translation. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/.

articles.title: Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide for HIV: a meta-analysis of efficacy across treatment-naïve and experienced populations and comparative effectiveness versus dolutegravir/lamivudine.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (BIC/FTC/TAF) is a preferred single-tablet regimen for HIV treatment, but head-to-head meta-analytic comparisons between treatment-experienced (TE) and treatment-naïve (TN) individuals are lacking. Additionally, the comparative effectiveness of BIC/FTC/TAF versus dolutegravir/lamivudine (DTG/3TC) remains to be systematically synthesized. We aimed to systematically compare the efficacy of BIC/FTC/TAF between TE and TN people with HIV, and evaluate the comparative effectiveness of BIC/FTC/TAF versus DTG/3TC. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Embase up to September 2026. Observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reporting virologic suppression or treatment discontinuation rates in both TE and TN populations receiving BIC/FTC/TAF, or BIC/FTC/TAF versus DTG/3TC were included. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Single-group proportion meta-analyses used a random-effects model, whereas comparative meta-analyses used the prespecified fixed-effect model. RESULTS: Thirty-one studies were included. For TE participants, the pooled virologic suppression rate was 95% (95% CI: 92%-97%) at 12 months, and for TN participants, the rate was 90% (95% CI: 85%-94%). In design-stratified comparative analyses between BIC/FTC/TAF and DTG/3TC, no statistically significant difference was detected in RCT (OR = 1.46, 95% CI: 0.80-2.66) or cohort studies (OR = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.70-1.39) among TN populations, nor in TE populations (RCT: OR = 1.04, 95% CI: 0.34-3.16; cohort: OR = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.42-2.02). No statistically significant differences were detected for treatment discontinuation (all-cause: OR = 1.02, 95% CI: 0.70-1.49; adverse events: OR = 1.11, 95% CI: 0.55-2.22). CONCLUSION: BIC/FTC/TAF achieves high virologic suppression rates and low discontinuation rates in both TE and TN populations, supporting its use as a first-line and switch option. BIC/FTC/TAF and DTG/3TC showed no statistically significant differences in virologic suppression or treatment discontinuation, suggesting both are viable guideline-preferred options. The choice between them should be individualized based on patient characteristics, including prior treatment history, adherence potential, comorbidity profile, and metabolic risk considerations.

articles.title: Differing roles of the calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and amylin receptors in migraine-related light aversion and gastrointestinal dysfunction in mice.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: The neuropeptide calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) is a well-established player in migraine. Current CGRP migraine therapeutics were designed to inhibit the canonical CGRP receptor, yet, based on in vitro studies, they can also inhibit to a lesser degree the amylin receptor 1 (AMY1), which CGRP can also activate. This study explores the potential in vivo contributions of these receptors to migraine-like symptoms in mice. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Receptor contributions were probed using light aversion as a surrogate for photophobia and diarrhoea as a readout for gastrointestinal dysfunction in outbred CD1 mice. Induction of diarrhoea was also measured in C57BL/6 J mice. CGRP and amylin were used as agonists, with two selective antagonists, olcegepant for the canonical CGRP receptor and AC187 for calcitonin receptor (CT)-based receptors, including AMY1. KEY RESULTS: CGRP and amylin induced light aversion in CD1 mice and diarrhoea in both strains. CGRP-induced light aversion was partially rescued by AC187, but not olcegepant. Light aversion was fully rescued only by a combination of AC187 and olcegepant. In contrast, olcegepant fully blocked CGRP-induced diarrhoea, while AC187 only partially blocked at high doses. As a control, olcegepant fully rescued CGRP-induced periorbital touch hypersensitivity in CD1 mice. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: More than one receptor contributes to CGRP-induced light aversion, with a CT-based receptor unexpectedly playing a major role. In contrast, the canonical CGRP receptor plays a major role in CGRP-induced diarrhoea. Thus, targeting a CT-based receptor may reduce photophobia with less adverse gastrointestinal effects in migraine patients.

articles.title: Cancer vaccine development gets complicated.
How can gene therapy platforms be scaled up to treat thousands of rare diseases?
Hypoxia-responsive CAIX-targeted radioligand for non-invasive imaging and radioligand therapy: from preclinical to first-in-human evaluation.
articles.abstract: Carbonic anhydrase IX (CAIX) is an attractive target for radioligand theranostics because it is constitutively overexpressed in clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and induced by hypoxia in several solid tumors. Existing CAIX-targeted radiotracers are constrained by delayed imaging kinetics, limited tumor retention, incomplete therapeutic-labeling compatibility, or insufficient tumor-to-background contrast. Here we report GL-261, a CAIX-targeted radioligand that appends a nitroimidazole bioreductive retention module to a CAIX-targeting pharmacophore within a DOTA-chelated scaffold. This design enables paired radiolabeling with gallium-68 for PET imaging and lutetium-177 for radioligand therapy. Nitroimidazole conjugation conferred hypoxia-dependent cellular accumulation, greater internalization (64.6% versus 45.2%), and higher CAIX-dependent tumor uptake than the comparator DPI-4452 without compromising target specificity. In xenograft models spanning different CAIX expression levels, [68Ga]Ga-GL-261 PET stratified tumors by CAIX status and was suppressed by receptor blocking. [177Lu]Lu-GL-261 showed sustained tumor retention over 168h and, at 37 MBq, produced marked tumor growth suppression without overt hematological or organ toxicity. In a first-in-human PET/CT study of 15 patients, [68Ga]Ga-GL-261 showed reproducible biodistribution, an effective dose of 8.45 × 10-2mSv/MBq, and lesion uptake that correlated with CAIX immunohistochemical expression (r = 0.93, P = 0.007 at 60min). These findings support hypoxia-responsive modification as a design strategy for CAIX-targeted radioligands and provide a translational basis for GL-261 in CAIX-expressing cancers. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Chinese Clinical Trail (registration No. ChiCTR2600127500).

articles.title: Targeting the SND1-MTDH/FANCD2 axis impairs DNA repair and sensitizes triple-negative breast cancer to PARP inhibitor.
articles.abstract: Although the staphylococcal nuclease domain-containing protein 1 (SND1)-metadherin (MTDH) complex is a promising therapeutic target in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), its role in DNA damage repair (DDR) remains unclear. Here, we identified FANCD2 as a previously unrecognized downstream effector of the SND1-MTDH complex. SND1 and MTDH cooperate to stabilize FANCD2 mRNA, thereby sustaining FANCD2 expression and DDR in TNBC cells. Guided by our finding, we designed DP3, an MTDH-derived peptide inhibitor that binds SND1 with high affinity and selectively disrupts the SND1-MTDH interaction. DP3 promoted degradation of both SND1 and MTDH, destabilized FANCD2 mRNA, reduced FANCD2 expression, and consequently increased DNA damage accumulation. Functionally, DP3 suppressed TNBC cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and survival and showed potent antitumor activity in patient-derived organoids and xenograft models, with a favorable safety profile in vivo. Importantly, DP3 enhanced the antitumor activity of PARP inhibitors (PARPi) in TNBC models by further suppressing FANCD2 expression and promoting DNA damage accumulation. These findings identify the SND1-MTDH/FANCD2 axis as a previously unrecognized regulator of DDR and PARPi sensitivity and provide a rationale for combining SND1-MTDH interaction inhibitors with PARPi in TNBC.

articles.title: An oral delivery platform for protein drugs: PDA/PEGylated engineered probiotics responsively release TLR5 agonists to prevent radiation enteritis.
articles.abstract: Oral protein delivery is hindered by gastrointestinal degradation and poor mucosal bioavailability. Engineered probiotics offer a promising strategy for oral protein delivery, but their therapeutic efficacy is often limited by insufficient payload expression and low secretion efficiency. Here, we present a living oral platform that integrates high-yield protein biosynthesis with on-demand intestinal release. By gene manipulation and FLAG tagging, we dramatically upregulate constitutive expression of GP532 in probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), while installing an arabinose-inducible autolytic switch for efficient intracellular payload release. A dual-layer coating of polydopamine (PDA) and polyethylene glycol (PEG) confers acid resistance and mucus penetration, while allowing arabinose to permeate and blocking digestive enzymes. Upon single oral gavage in a murine model of radiation enteritis, our formulation achieves therapeutic efficacy fully equivalent to systemic injection of GP532 in mitigating intestinal injury. Critically, unlike injectable biologics, this living platform promotes the restoration of gut microbial community structure and beneficial taxa, a unique benefit unattainable by parenteral administration, while the engineered strain is completely cleared within 24 h. By synergizing genetic circuit engineering, surface chemical modification, and in situ luminal release, this work establishes a single-dose, orally effective alternative to injectable protein therapy, offering a transformative strategy for the prevention of radiation enteritis with the added benefit of microbiome maintenance.

articles.title: Dissolving microneedle patches for needle-free and thermostable respiratory syncytial virus vaccination.
articles.abstract: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) remains a major cause of acute lower respiratory tract disease, yet current prefusion F (preF)-based RSV vaccines depend on intramuscular injection and cold-chain distribution, limiting broad deployment. Dissolving microneedle array patches (MAPs) offer a minimally invasive, needle-free, and potentially thermostable alternative to conventional vaccine delivery. Here, we developed dissolving microneedle array patches loaded with an engineered prefusion-stabilized RSV F antigen (CL073A) and evaluated their potential as a needle-free, thermostable, and potent RSV vaccination platform. Following formulation screening, two lead CL073A-loaded MAPs (MAPs-CL073A) were identified that preserved antigenicity and mechanical performance and showed prolonged local antigen retention relative to intramuscular injection. In mice, MAPs-CL073A elicited markedly enhanced and durable humoral immunity, inducing approximately five-fold higher neutralizing antibody titers than intramuscular immunization at a ten-fold lower antigen dose, demonstrating a pronounced dose-sparing effect. In cotton rats, MAPs-CL073A conferred robust protection against RSV challenge by reducing lung viral burden and pulmonary pathology, with the 10 μg regimen (F2-MAP) achieving near-complete protection. Furthermore, the patches fully retained antigen bioactivity and in vivo immunogenicity after 6 months of room-temperature storage. Our findings establish that antigen delivery is a critical dimension of RSV vaccine performance and support dissolving microneedle delivery as a versatile strategy to enhance both the efficacy and deployability of RSV vaccines.

articles.title: Copper dysregulation and ferroptotic vulnerability in Wilson disease: Mechanistic evidence and therapeutic potential of plant-derived natural compounds.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: ATP7B dysfunction in Wilson disease (WD) disrupts copper homeostasis and promotes mitochondrial injury, altered iron handling, and oxidative lipid damage. Whether these changes culminate in ferroptotic cell death, and whether plant-derived compounds provide ferroptosis-dependent protection, remain unresolved. PURPOSE: To critically examine the mechanistic basis of ferroptotic vulnerability in WD and assess the evidence and translational potential of chemically defined plant-derived compounds. METHODS: PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, Embase, and Scopus were searched from inception through 16 September 2026. Eligible experimental studies were assessed for methodological limitations and disease-model fidelity, and mechanistic evidence was graded using a review-specific cumulative four-level framework. Findings were synthesized narratively alongside contextual mechanistic, pharmacokinetic, and safety literature. RESULTS: Seven preclinical studies evaluating curcumin, ferulic acid, diosgenin, berberine, aloe-emodin, quercetin, and polydatin were included. Reported protection in hepatic, neural, or ovarian models was accompanied by changes in copper handling, antioxidant defenses, and lipid metabolism. Six studies remained at Level 1 (ferroptosis-compatible evidence); only the polydatin study reached Level 2, providing functional pharmacological support with nonspecific endpoints. No study met the criteria for dependence on core ferroptosis machinery or convergent causal validation (Levels 3 and 4), and functional validation in human WD-derived systems was absent. Protection specifically attributable to ferroptosis suppression at matched copper burden remained unproven. Uncertain target-organ exposure and insufficient long-term safety and combination-treatment data further constrain translation. CONCLUSION: Plant-derived compounds warrant investigation as potential adjuncts to established copper-lowering therapy, but their ferroptosis-specific mechanisms and clinical benefit in WD remain unestablished. Copper-matched mechanistic studies, independent replication, and pharmacokinetic and safety evaluation are required to determine whether they offer additional organ protection.

articles.title: Multifunctional bioactive glass platforms for bone regeneration: from material design to microenvironment modulation.
articles.abstract: Bone defects caused by trauma, tumor resection, infection, and degenerative diseases remain a major clinical challenge, especially critical-sized defects that surpass the inherent regenerative capacity of native bone tissue. Conventional bone grafting approaches, including autologous and allogeneic bone transplantation, are widely adopted in clinical practice. Nevertheless, their applications are limited by donor-site morbidity, immune rejection, and insufficient donor supply. Bioactive glasses (BGs), a family of inorganic biomaterials, can initiate cascaded regenerative responses through surface reactions and tunable ion release, covering osteogenesis, angiogenesis and immunomodulation. Therefore, BGs have become promising candidates for bone repair. To date, various BG-based forms have been fabricated, ranging from nanoparticles and porous scaffolds to injectable systems and surface-modified implant coatings. This review summarizes recent advances of BG biomaterials for bone defect repair, with particular focus on ion-mediated biological mechanisms, material modification strategies, and microenvironment regulation. Additionally, we discuss major bottlenecks hindering their clinical translation and propose prospects for future research.

articles.title: Folate-functionalized chitosan nanoparticles for precision cancer therapy from nanoplatform design to clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Folic acid-functionalized chitosan nanoparticles (FA-CS-NPs) have emerged as one of the most extensively investigated active-targeting nanoplatforms for cancer therapy and have a non-immunogenic targeting capacity of folate-receptor engagement. This review consolidates recent advances in the design, functionalization, and therapeutic performance of FA-CS-NPs across a broad landscape of architectures, tumor microenvironment (TME)-responsive dual-stimuli systems, metal-organic framework (MOF) and mesoporous silica nanoplatforms, magnetic, carbon, and graphene-based multifunctional carriers, and biomimetic or green-synthesized redox-active biohybrids. Across these platforms, folate conjugation consistently improved folate-receptor-mediated cellular uptake, cytotoxic potency, and tumor-cell selectivity, allowing acid-triggered payload release within the acidic tumor and endolysosomal microenvironment. Chemotherapeutics, natural products, metal complexes, kinase inhibitors, photosensitizers, and biologics have been investigated using FA-CS-based nanocarriers with several studies reporting encouraging in vitro biocompatibility and preliminary safety findings in preclinical models. However, differences in toxicity endpoints, study duration and animal models limit broader conclusions regarding their long-term safety and clinical suitability. This review critically evaluates these limitations and emphasizes the need for standardized manufacturing, Quality-by-Design (QbD) frameworks, and receptor-guided patient classification in transforming FA-CS-NPs from experimental platforms to precision nanomedicines for cancer therapy.

articles.title: Mechanical microenvironment-guided smart nano drug delivery systems for pulmonary fibrosis: from fibrotic delivery barriers to therapeutic remodeling.
articles.abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is associated with excessive extracellular matrix (ECM) deposition and progressive changes in tissue mechanics, which sustain profibrotic signaling and create additional barriers to effective drug delivery. Fibrotic remodeling alters matrix architecture, interstitial transport, and cellular behavior, while heterogeneous ventilation, airway mucus, and pulmonary clearance further influence the distribution and retention of therapeutic agents. This review examines the mechanical microenvironment in PF and its implications for nanomedicine design. It considers how ECM remodeling, tissue stiffness, and cellular mechanotransduction contribute to disease development and persistence, including their interactions with profibrotic signaling pathways. The effects of structural and mechanical alterations in fibrotic lungs on drug transport and delivery are then examined. Nanomedicine strategies discussed include ECM-targeted and enzyme-assisted approaches to improve tissue penetration, strategies to enhance transport across airway mucus, targeted delivery to mechanically stressed epithelial cells and activated fibroblasts, macrophage-directed interventions, and disruption of pathological crosstalk between mechanical and biochemical signaling. These approaches are assessed in terms of delivery performance, antifibrotic efficacy, and experimental evidence supporting the modulation of cellular or tissue mechanical properties. Emerging mechanically responsive materials are also considered, particularly their potential to exploit mechanical deformation to regulate material function and transport behavior in drug delivery systems. Clinical progress and translational limitations are examined, with emphasis on the evidence needed to advance preclinical strategies toward clinical applications. Translation of mechanical microenvironment-guided nanomedicine will require clear evidence linking drug delivery to fibrotic lesions, modulation of pathological tissue mechanics, therapeutic efficacy, and long-term safety.

articles.title: Context-dependent regulation of lipid homeostasis by miR-122: Molecular mechanisms, disease relevance, and therapeutic implications.
articles.abstract: miR-122 is a liver-enriched microRNA that shapes systemic lipid homeostasis by coordinating hepatic de novo lipogenesis, oxidative disposal, intracellular storage, and lipoprotein export. Mechanistically, miR-122 intersects with energy-sensing pathways centered on AMPK, modulates lipogenesis through Sirtuin-LKB1/AMPK control, influences triglyceride handling via YY1-linked transcriptional programs, and engages noncoding RNA circuits that regulate autophagy. Furthermore, intracellular miR-122 regulates lipid peroxidation (ferroptosis) in a highly context-dependent manner: it buffers against oxidative injury in steatotic hepatocytes and ischemic tissue injuries, yet actively promotes ferroptosis by targeting SLC7A11 and GPX4 in hepatocellular carcinoma and autoimmune hepatitis. Meanwhile, extracellular vesicle (EV)-associated miR-122 mediates pathogenic inter-organ metabolic communication. Clinically, the progressive decline of hepatic miR-122 drives the transition from simple steatosis to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), positioning circulating miR-122 as a highly sensitive diagnostic biomarker. Short-term antagonism via locked nucleic acid (LNA)-based anti-miRs efficiently lowers circulating cholesterol, yet preclinical models suggest that prolonged suppression risks progressive hepatic inflammatory remodeling and steatofibrosis. Conversely, for advanced liver diseases characterized by miR-122 depletion, miR-122 replacement therapies show potential to restore metabolic resilience and suppress fibrogenesis. This review synthesizes current mechanistic evidence and highlights the development of miR-122-targeted nucleic acid drugs and the therapeutic exploitation of exosomal vectors, providing a translational scene for managing lipid-driven metabolic and hepatic disorders.

articles.title: Extracellular vesicles in viral myocarditis: Mechanisms, biomarkers and emerging therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Viral myocarditis (VM) is an inflammatory heart disease most commonly triggered by viral infection and represents a major cause of acute cardiac dysfunction and chronic inflammatory cardiomyopathy. Although cardiomyocyte injury and immune activation are central to VM pathogenesis, the mechanisms by which viral infection coordinates intercellular communication to drive disease progression remain incompletely understood. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as key mediators of cell-to-cell signaling, capable of transporting viral components and host-derived factors that modulate immune responses and cardiac function. In this review, we integrate preclinical and clinical evidence to define the mechanistic roles of EVs in VM and evaluate their translational potential. We highlight circulating EVs as minimally invasive biomarkers for early diagnosis and disease monitoring. We further discuss emerging strategies to therapeutically target or engineer EVs to modulate both viral replication and maladaptive host responses.

articles.title: α-pinene and the central nervous system: Mechanistic insights, preclinical evidence, and translational perspectives.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: α-Pinene is a naturally occurring monoterpene that has attracted increasing interest for its potential effects on the central nervous system (CNS). This review critically evaluates preclinical evidence regarding its effects on neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, neurotrophic signaling, cellular injury, and behavioral outcomes. METHODS: A literature search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar from database inception to April 2026. Studies investigating CNS-related effects of α-pinene, including in vitro and in vivo experimental studies, were narratively synthesized according to biological mechanisms, experimental models, doses, administration routes, treatment duration, and outcomes. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or quantitative meta-analysis was performed. RESULTS: Preclinical evidence indicates that α-pinene is associated with attenuation of inflammatory signaling, particularly TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB-related responses, and reduction of oxidative stress accompanied by enhanced endogenous antioxidant defenses. Modulation of BDNF/TrkB/CREB-associated signaling has also been reported, although evidence is more limited and context-dependent. Additional studies suggest effects on apoptosis-related signaling, glial activation, inflammasome-associated pathways, JNK signaling, and endoplasmic reticulum stress. Behavioral studies report anxiolytic-like, cognitive, anticonvulsant, motor-protective, and analgesic effects in several experimental models. However, dose-response and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic relationships remain insufficiently characterized, and some findings are model-dependent. CONCLUSION: Current evidence supports α-pinene as a biologically active monoterpene with CNS-related effects predominantly demonstrated in preclinical models. A single validated molecular mechanism, therapeutic dose range, or human CNS therapeutic window has not been established. Further independent replication, standardized dose-response studies, brain-exposure profiling, mechanistic validation, and long-term safety studies are required before clinical translation can be considered.

articles.title: Can a generalizable dose-effect relationship be inferred for cannabidiol? Evidence from the preclinical literature.
articles.abstract: RATIONALE: Cannabidiol (CBD) modulates anxiety and fear in rodents; however, the dose-dependent characteristics of these effects remain unclear. OBJECTIVES & METHODS: Regression-based analyses assessed how consistent dose-effect inferences are across diverse studies and determined whether linear or nonlinear models best describe the relationship between CBD dose and behavioral outcomes. Hedges' g effect sizes from 312 experiments in mice and rats were analyzed separately and in pooled datasets, using both raw and allometrically normalized doses. We also evaluated how biological and procedural variables moderated dose-effect relationships. RESULTS: Intermediate doses of systemic CBD administration were more often associated with larger antiaversive effect sizes; however, this trend did not hold across species or behavioral domains. Some analyses showed nonlinear trends, primarily associated with high-dose observations. After allometric scaling and pooling of anxiety and conditioned fear datasets, linear models fit better than nonlinear models. Analyses of pooled and anxiety datasets revealed no significant moderators of the dose-effect relationship. In contrast, analyses limited to conditioned fear identified species as a significant moderator, while sex, stress history, treatment regimen, age, and treatment-testing interval were not significant. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate that the preclinical literature does not support a stable or generalizable CBD dose-effect function. The observed relationships likely reflect substantial methodological heterogeneity and may also reflect CBD's pharmacological complexity. Factorial studies with balanced dose distributions and controlled experimental conditions are necessary to improve reproducibility and mechanistic understanding of CBD's antiversive effects.

articles.title: Beyond monoamines: a multi-systems molecular framework for major depressive disorder.
articles.abstract: For over five decades, the monoamine hypothesis has anchored the conceptual and pharmacological approach to major depressive disorder (MDD), yet nearly one-third of patients fail to achieve remission with standard antidepressants, and therapeutic response is delayed by weeks. This narrative review offers a critical synthesis of recent high-impact literature drawn on evidence from genomic, molecular, and translational studies across six domains: genomic architecture, epigenetic dysregulation, neuroinflammation, neurotrophic signalling, gut-brain axis, and rapid-acting antidepressant mechanisms, to construct a multi-systems framework of MDD pathophysiology and, as a secondary and explicitly scoped aim, to identify translational priorities for South Asian, particularly Indian, populations; the evidence reviewed is global in scope. A 2025 genome-wide association study (GWAS) of 688,808 cases identified 697 independent associations mapping to 635 genomic risk loci implicating glutamatergic, GABAergic, and neuropeptidergic systems. Environmental stressors converge on this genetic susceptibility through DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNA-mediated epigenetic reprogramming. An inflammatory MDD subgroup, characterised by kynurenine pathway disruption and microglial dysregulation, is of interest for patient stratification. Rapid-acting antidepressants proposed to act through TrkB-BDNF-dependent synaptic plasticity offer a mechanistic account of their fast onset, although the direct-binding theory awaits independent replication. Gut microbiome dysbiosis, particularly among neurotransmitter-producing taxa, further extends the pathophysiological map beyond the brain itself. Together, these findings support a shift from a unidimensional monoaminergic model to an integrated, multi-systems molecular framework of MDD. Realising the clinical potential of this framework will require validated precision biomarker panels, dedicated South Asian GWAS cohorts, and longitudinal multi-omics studies.

articles.title: Neuropharmacology of omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids in neurodegenerative diseases: mechanisms, multi-omics evidence, and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, involve progressive neuronal dysfunction associated with neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial impairment, defective proteostasis, and synaptic failure. Although symptomatic treatment remains central, anti-amyloid therapies can modestly slow clinical decline in selected patients with early Alzheimer's disease. This review critically evaluates the neuropharmacological evidence for omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, particularly docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), and the barriers to their clinical translation. We narratively synthesized preclinical, observational, and interventional clinical evidence, focusing on membrane organization, inflammatory resolution, mitochondrial and redox homeostasis, autophagy, proteostasis, neuronal signaling, and factors contributing to heterogeneous clinical outcomes. Preclinical studies support context-dependent effects of DHA and EPA on neuronal membranes, inflammatory signaling, mitochondrial function, redox balance, autophagy, and synaptic plasticity. Human evidence is less consistent: observational studies generally report favorable associations between omega-3 status and neurological outcomes, whereas randomized trials show null, modest, or subgroup-dependent effects. Outcomes vary with disease stage, baseline omega-3 status, formulation, dose, treatment duration, genotype, and endpoint selection. Uncertain central nervous system exposure and limited pharmacokinetic and target-engagement data remain major translational barriers. Omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids are biologically plausible neuropharmacological modulators, but current evidence does not establish DHA or EPA as broadly effective disease-modifying treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. Future trials should prioritize early-stage, biomarker-stratified populations, pharmacologically characterized formulations, adequate treatment duration, and clinically meaningful progression-related outcomes.

articles.title: Atorvastatin-associated liver injury: a structured narrative review of reporting signals, clinical phenotypes, and hepatic safety, 2023-2026.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Atorvastatin is widely prescribed, yet its hepatic safety remains debated: randomized trials and biopsy-proven cohorts indicate acceptable safety, whereas pharmacovigilance data and case reports describe injury ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to acute liver failure. METHODS: PubMed was searched for records combining atorvastatin terms with liver-injury concepts, published 1 July 2023 to 31 July 2026; records were screened in duplicate and assigned to one of four outcome domains-biochemical liver test abnormality, suspected drug-induced liver injury (DILI), clinically significant or severe DILI, and acute liver failure-and were not combined across domains. This is a structured narrative review, not a systematic review: only PubMed was searched and comprehensive retrieval is not claimed. RESULTS: Of 119 records, 57 were included in the synthesis: 31 directly addressed atorvastatin and liver injury and 26 addressed statin hepatic safety or statin use in chronic liver disease. Among 7,779 statin-associated drug-induced liver injury (DILI) cases in FAERS (2004-2023), atorvastatin accounted for 53.48%, with a reporting odds ratio of 3.09. In 1 211 reported Chinese cases of statin-associated liver injury, the odds of severe injury were 1.77-fold higher with atorvastatin than with rosuvastatin, and 2.08-fold higher with combination therapy than with statin monotherapy. Phenotypes included hepatocellular, cholestatic and mixed injury, drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH) and hyperacute liver failure, usually within 2-3 months. Rechallenge reproduced injury in 12 of 16 cases, with median latency shortened from 27 to 11 days, whereas switching to a hydrophilic statin was usually tolerated. Mechanisms involve mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, CYP3A-mediated metabolic activation, bile-acid transporter inhibition and pharmacogenomic variation. Conversely, in MASLD and cirrhosis, atorvastatin did not worsen liver injury and reduced liver-related events. CONCLUSION: Severe atorvastatin-associated liver injury is rare but recognizable. Structured monitoring, causality assessment and injury phenotyping are essential, same-drug rechallenge should be avoided, and hydrophilic statins preferred. Statin therapy should not be withheld in chronic liver disease.

articles.title: Microbial metabolites in chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment: from mechanistic associations to pharmacological target validation.
articles.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment (CICI) encompasses heterogeneous changes in memory, attention, executive function and processing speed. Microbial metabolites offer experimentally tractable candidates because their exposure, dose-response relationships and host-target engagement can be measured. This review evaluates short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), microbial indoles and host kynurenine metabolism, and microbially modified bile acids, while considering microbial inflammatory products as distinct modifiers of the intestinal-brain environment. Evidence is assessed against five criteria: CICI specificity, temporal sequence, selective causal manipulation, host-target engagement and oncological compatibility. Clinical microbiome associations and probiotic intervention findings support further investigation, but do not establish mediation by an individual metabolite. Selected chemotherapy models provide cognitive and molecular intervention evidence, although its strength varies by agent, metabolic pathway and behavioral endpoint. Changes in metabolite concentrations may reflect altered diet, epithelial absorption, host metabolism or clearance as well as microbial production. Translation therefore requires regimen-specific longitudinal sampling, compartment- appropriate exposure measurements, selective pathway perturbation and domain-specific cognitive assessment with controls for sickness and motor impairment. Cognitive protection must also be evaluated alongside chemotherapy exposure, tumor control and infectious safety. This framework distinguishes biomarkers of treatment-associated injury from causal mediators and identifies the evidence needed to develop metabolite-guided pharmacological interventions.

articles.title: Pharmacological strategies to manage oxidative stress in Huntington's disease: from preclinical models to clinical trials.
articles.abstract: Huntington disease (HD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder for which effective disease-modifying treatments remain limited. Growing evidence indicates that oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired cellular antioxidant responses are important contributors to HD pathogenesis and may interact with mechanisms that drive disease progression, including somatic CAG repeat expansion. This narrative review examines therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring redox balance in HD, with particular emphasis on approaches targeting mitochondrial function, antioxidant defense, glutathione metabolism, lipid oxidation, and metal homeostasis. Although a broad range of compounds has shown beneficial effects in experimental models, translation into clinical benefit has so far been limited. This gap may reflect insufficient target engagement, inadequate brain exposure, intervention at advanced disease stages, and the difficulty of capturing biologically meaningful effects using conventional clinical endpoints. Future therapeutic development may therefore benefit from earlier intervention, biomarker-guided patient stratification, combination strategies integrating redox modulation with huntingtin-lowering approaches, and the repurposing of clinically established drugs targeting mitochondrial and redox pathways.

articles.title: Bioactive metabolites and botanical preparations from plants used as medicines and foods in ulcerative colitis: a mechanism-oriented narrative review of multi-target regulation.
articles.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic relapsing inflammatory bowel disease with a complex pathophysiology involving immune dysregulation, gut microbiota dysbiosis, intestinal barrier impairment, oxidative stress, and regulated cell death. Current therapeutic strategies, including 5-aminosalicylic acid, corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, biologics, and small-molecule agents, have improved disease management; however, incomplete or lost response, adverse effects, and the need for long-term treatment remain important clinical challenges. Bioactive metabolites and botanical preparations from medicinal and food plants have gained increasing attention because of their diverse pharmacological activities and potential to modulate multiple pathological processes involved in UC. This mechanism-oriented narrative review critically summarizes recent evidence on the effects of these plant-derived metabolites, botanical preparations, and combination strategies in UC using a framework that links major UC pathological modules to molecular targets/pathways and functional outcomes, with particular emphasis on anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions, regulation of ferroptosis and pyroptosis, modulation of autophagy and endoplasmic reticulum stress, protection of the intestinal barrier, and regulation of gut microbiota. The reported mechanisms recurrently converge on signaling networks involving NF-κB, MAPK, Nrf2/ARE, and PI3K/Akt. Evidence from isolated-metabolite cellular studies, extract- and preparation-level studies, animal models, and available human studies varies by the study type. We interpret it according to its mechanistic and translational relevance. Although the available literature indicates that these metabolites may regulate interconnected UC-related pathways through multi-target actions, most mechanistic evidence remains preclinical. Important limitations include incomplete reporting of dose ranges, controls, sample sizes, and quantitative effect estimates; inconsistent documentation of taxonomic authentication and extract characterization; limited metabolite-specific pharmacokinetic and bioavailability data; insufficient translational validation of advanced delivery strategies; variability in microbiota-related findings among experimental models; and limited clinical validation. Further well-designed pharmacological and clinical studies are required to clarify the most robust mechanisms and identify plant-derived metabolites with the greatest potential for further development in UC.

articles.title: Efficacy and safety of anisodamine as adjuvant therapy in septic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Some patients with septic shock still exhibit microcirculatory dysfunction and impaired tissue oxygen metabolism (macro-micro dissociation), even when macrohemodynamic targets are achieved. Anisodamine may improve patients' symptoms through multiple mechanisms, including anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects mediated by the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway and the relief of microvascular spasm; however, the quality of existing evidence is variable. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of anisodamine as adjuvant therapy for septic shock. METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Embase, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang Data, and the VIP database from inception to 1 June 2026. RCTs comparing anisodamine with control in septic shock were included. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, and the certainty of evidence was rated using the GRADE approach. RESULTS: A total of 14 RCTs (2 in English and 12 in Chinese) were included. Compared with control, anisodamine reduced 28-day mortality (6 studies; RR = 0.76; 95% CI, 0.62-0.93). Anisodamine also significantly increased mean arterial pressure (MD = 3.92; 95% CI, 1.85-5.98) and the systemic vascular resistance index (MD = 74.78; 95% CI, 17.59-131.97). Furthermore, anisodamine increased the Lactate clearance rate (MD = 16.27; 95% CI, 9.26-23.28), reduced serum Lactate (MD = -0.68; 95% CI, -1.10 to -0.26), and increased oxygen consumption (VO2; MD = 23.10; 95% CI, 11.53-34.68) without increasing oxygen delivery (DO2). Anisodamine also reduced the SOFA score (MD = -1.17; 95% CI, -1.95 to -0.39) and the APACHE-II score (MD = -1.50; 95% CI, -2.34 to -0.65), and shortened the duration of vasoactive agent use, ICU length of stay (LOS), and duration of mechanical ventilation, although the total hospital LOS was unchanged. Heart rate was similar between groups based on limited data. However, adverse events were under-reported across studies, and cardiac safety of anisodamine could not be reliably assessed from the available evidence. CONCLUSION: Anisodamine as an adjuvant therapy for septic shock may reduce 28-day mortality and improve certain macrocirculatory hemodynamic parameters, tissue perfusion, oxygen metabolism, and organ function indicators. A microcirculatory mechanism is plausible but remains unproven, as no direct microcirculatory endpoint could be pooled. In addition, given that the included studies were mostly small-sample trials with substantial heterogeneity and limited certainty of evidence, large-sample, multicenter RCTs are needed (ideally focusing more on microcirculatory indicators) to further clarify the mechanism, optimal dose, timing, and appropriate treatment population.

articles.title: TALK-1 and TALK-2 channels in pancreatic β-cell function.
articles.abstract: Diabetes is a major non-communicable disease in which impaired insulin secretion contributes to loss of glucose homeostasis. ATP-sensitive K+ (KATP) channels couple glucose metabolism to β-cell electrical activity and are established therapeutic targets. However, KATP-dependent depolarization alone does not fully explain the regulation of insulin secretion. Emerging evidence identifies the two-pore-domain K+ channels TALK-1 and TALK-2 as additional regulators of β-cell function. This Mini Review integrates genetic, mechanistic, and pharmacological evidence to examine how TALK channels regulate β-cell function and to distinguish established cellular effects from unresolved implications for diabetes. TALK-1 studies link membrane excitability, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ homeostasis, and mitochondrial function to secretory regulation, while disease-associated variants support its relevance to diabetes. Recent human islet experiments show that TALK-2 regulates ER Ca2+ handling and modulates basal insulin release and the secretory response to glucose. Together, these findings indicate that the secretory consequences of TALK channel modulation depend on glucose availability and metabolic context. Selective TALK-1 inhibitors provide tools to test mechanisms previously investigated mainly through genetic manipulation.
